english_title: Ye Jo Halka Halka Suroor Hai
urdu_title: یہ جو ہلکا ہلکا سرور ہے
overall_summary: This qawwali is one of the most beloved compositions in the Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan canon, built around the central Sufi metaphor of divine intoxication — the lover rendered helplessly drunk not by wine but by the gaze of the Beloved. The poet Abdul Hameed Adam weaves together the classical Persian-Urdu imagery of the saqi, the rind, the zahid, and the maikhanah to construct a spiritual world in which all conventional religious obligation dissolves in the face of ishq. The qawwali moves through multiple emotional registers — playful, ecstatic, defiant, tender, heartbroken, and finally comic — reflecting the full arc of the mystic lover's experience. Nusrat's performance extends and deepens the written poem through improvisation, repetition, and the insertion of additional verses, transforming it into a living spiritual event rather than a recitation.

sections.urdu_text:

sections.romanization:
Saqi ki har nigah pe bal kha ke pi gaya
Lehron se khelta hua lehra ke pi gaya
Ae rehmat-e-tamam, meri har khata maaf
Main intiha-e-shauq mein ghabra ke pi gaya
Ae rehmat-e-tamam, meri har khata maaf
Main intiha-e-shauq mein ghabra ke pi gaya
Pita baghair izn, pita baghair izn, yeh kab thi meri majaal?
Dar parda chashm-e-yaar ki shah pa ke pi gaya
Zahid yeh meri shokhiye rindan na dekh na

sections.translation:
At every glance of the saqi, I swayed and drank
Playing upon the waves, swirling, I drank
O mercy of the universe, forgive my every transgression
In the extremity of my longing, overwhelmed, I drank
O mercy of the universe, forgive my every transgression
In the extremity of my longing, overwhelmed, I drank
Drinking without permission — when was this ever within my power?
I found encouragement in the secret glance of my Beloved's eye, and drank
O ascetic, do not look upon this audacity of mine, this rind-like boldness
I shattered my vow of repentance to pieces, and trembling, I drank
sections.explanation: This opening verse establishes the entire spiritual universe of the qawwali in a single sweep. The saqi — the divine cupbearer, a figure for God or the spiritual master — does not force the wine upon the lover; a single glance is enough to make him sway and drink. The repeated plea 'ae rehmat-e-tamam, meri har khata maaf' is extraordinary in its audacity: the lover acknowledges his transgression of drinking without permission, yet immediately reveals that the permission was granted covertly through the Beloved's own secret glance — making God both the prohibition and the invitation simultaneously. The zahid couplet draws on one of the oldest tensions in Sufi poetry: the dry, legalistic ascetic who cannot understand that the rind's apparent transgression is in fact the deepest form of surrender. The word 'thrra ke' — trembling — is crucial: this is not defiant drinking but awed, overwhelmed drinking, the soul shaking before the magnitude of divine love.

sections.romanization:
Audi audi ghatayen aati hain
Mutribon ki nawayen aati hain
Kis ke gesu khule hain sawan mein?
Mehki mehki hawayen aati hain
Aao seene chaman mein raqs karen

sections.translation:
Dark, dark monsoon clouds are rolling in
The melodies of the musicians are drifting near
Whose tresses have come undone in the season of rain?
Fragrant, fragrant breezes are breathing through
Come, let us dance in the garden of the heart
The clouds arrive bearing music within them
sections.explanation: This verse is a classical baramasa — a seasonal poem — in miniature, using the monsoon as a metaphor for the descent of divine grace and spiritual longing. The dark clouds in Urdu and Punjabi poetry are among the most potent symbols of the beloved's hair, of melancholy sweetness, and of the rains of mercy that revive the parched earth of the lover's heart. The question 'whose tresses have come undone in the sawan?' is deliberately unanswered — in Sufi poetry this ambiguity is intentional, the loose hair suggesting both the earthly beloved and the divine mystery unveiled. The invitation to dance in the garden of the heart places the whirling of sama — the devotional practice of the Sufis — within the inner landscape of the soul itself.

sections.urdu_text:

sections.romanization:
Dekh kar un ki aankhon ko karhne walon ko hayaen aati hain
Paas rehta hai door rehta hai, koi dil mein zaroor rehta hai
Jab se dekha hai teri aankhon ko halka halka suroor rehta hai
Aise rehte hain wo mere dil mein jaise zulmat mein noor rehta hai
Ab adam ka yeh haal hai har waqt mast rehta hai choor rehta hai
sections.translation:
Upon seeing those eyes, even those who burn with longing are overcome with shyness
Near yet far, yet someone most certainly dwells within this heart
Ever since I beheld your eyes, a gentle, gentle intoxication lingers
They dwell in my heart the way light dwells within darkness
Now this is Adam's state — forever intoxicated, forever undone
sections.explanation: This verse is the emotional and philosophical hinge of the qawwali, introducing the central image of halka halka suroor — the light, gentle, persistent intoxication that is not the crash of wine but the slow, permanent alteration of the soul transformed by divine vision. The paradox of 'paas rehta hai, door rehta hai' — near yet far — is one of the oldest formulations of the Sufi experience of God: the divine is simultaneously more intimate than one's own heartbeat and infinitely beyond reach. The final line uses the poet's pen name Adam (also meaning non-existence, عدم), a classical makhlas device that collapses the poet's identity into the state of fana — perpetual intoxication, perpetual dissolution.

sections.urdu_text:
یہ جو ہلکا ہلکا سرور ہے
یہ تِری نظر کا قصور ہے
کہ شراب پینا سکھا دیا
sections.romanization:
Yeh jo halka halka suroor hai
Yeh teri nazar ka qasoor hai
Keh sharaab peena sikha diya
sections.translation:
This gentle, gentle intoxication that lingers —
This is the fault of your gaze
That taught me how to drink
sections.explanation: The refrain is the master stroke of the poem — the word 'qasoor' (fault, blame) is used with exquisite irony. The lover does not blame the Beloved in anger but in ecstatic gratitude: it is your fault that I am now permanently intoxicated, your fault that I have learned the art of divine love. The teaching of drinking — 'sikha diya' — frames the entire spiritual journey as an education received from the gaze of God, not from books or mosques or religious instruction. In qawwali performance this refrain functions as the structural anchor, returning again and again to deepen with each repetition.

sections.urdu_text:
تِرے پیار نے، تِری چاہ نے
تِری بہکی بہکی نگاہ نے
مجھے اِک شرابی بنا دیا
sections.romanization:
Tere pyaar ne, teri chaah ne
Teri bahki bahki nigah ne
Mujhe ik sharabi bana diya
sections.translation:
Your love, your longing for me
Your reeling, reeling glance
Made of me a drunkard complete
sections.explanation: This verse escalates the central metaphor: the lover has not merely been taught to drink — he has been made into a drunkard, his very identity transformed. The word 'bahki bahki' (reeling, intoxicating, unsteady) applied to the Beloved's glance is remarkable — it suggests that the divine gaze itself is not serene but intoxicated, as if God looks upon the lover with the same overwhelming love that the lover feels. This reciprocity of divine intoxication is a distinctly Sufi theological position: the love between God and the soul is mutual and equal in its intensity.

sections.urdu_text:
شراب کیسی، خمار کیسا، یہ سب تمہاری نوازشیں ہیں
پلائی ہے کس نظر سے تُو نے کہ مجھ کو اپنی خبر نہیں ہے
تِری بہکی بہکی نگاہ نے، مجھے اِک شرابی بنا دیا
sections.romanization:
Sharaab kaisi, khumaar kaisa, yeh sab tumhari nawaazishen hain
Pilaai hai kis nazar se tu ne keh mujh ko apni khabar nahin hai
Teri bahki bahki nigah ne, mujhe ik sharabi bana diya
sections.translation:
What wine is this, what intoxication is this — all of it is your grace
With what kind of gaze have you given me to drink, that I have lost all awareness of myself
Your reeling, reeling glance has made of me a drunkard complete
sections.explanation: The lover now questions the very nature of his intoxication — not with doubt but with wonder. This is the hal of hayra (bewilderment), one of the highest stations in Sufi spiritual experience, in which the mystic is so overwhelmed by divine manifestation that all categories dissolve. The loss of self-awareness — 'mujh ko apni khabar nahin' — is not madness but the classical Sufi state of fana fi'llah, annihilation in God, the disappearance of the nafs (ego-self) in the ocean of divine presence. The verse closes by returning to the bahki nigah line, anchoring this ecstatic dissolution firmly in the transformative power of the Beloved's gaze.

sections.romanization:
Sara jahan mast, jahan ka nizam mast
Din mast, raat mast, sahar mast, shaam mast
Khum mast, shisha mast, subu mast, jaam mast
Yeh teri chashm-e-mast se har khasaan mast
Yun to saqi har tarah ki tere maikhanay mein hai

Teri bahki bahki nigah ne, mujhe ik sharabi bana diya
sections.translation:
The whole world is intoxicated, the very order of existence is intoxicated
Day intoxicated, night intoxicated, dawn intoxicated, dusk intoxicated
The wine jar intoxicated, the glass intoxicated, the flask intoxicated, the cup intoxicated
From your intoxicated eye, every one of the chosen elect is intoxicated
Your tavern holds every kind of wine, O saqi
Including that little which lives in the goblet of these eyes
I understand all your coquetry, O saqi
It is the glance that does the work — the goblet is merely its name
Your reeling, reeling glance has made of me a drunkard complete
sections.explanation: This is the most cosmologically ambitious verse of the qawwali — an ecstatic catalogue in which the intoxication spreads outward from the lover to encompass all of creation. The Sufi concept being expressed is wahdat al-wujud (unity of being): if the divine wine permeates everything, then everything exists in a state of divine intoxication, from the cosmic order (nizam) down to the smallest cup (jaam). The line about the khasan — the chosen saints and the spiritually elect — being rendered mast by the divine gaze is a powerful equalizer: even the greatest awliya cannot resist this intoxication. The closing insight — 'kaam karti hai nazar, naam hai paimanay ka' — is one of the most philosophically dense lines in the poem: the goblet is merely a name, a form; it is the gaze that is the actual agent of intoxication. Form is nothing; the divine look is everything.

sections.romanization:
Tera pyaar hai meri zindagi
Na namaaz aati hai mujh ko na wuzu aata hai
Sajda kar leta hun jab saamne tu aata hai

sections.translation:
Your love is my life entire
I know neither how to pray nor how to perform ablution
Yet I prostrate myself whenever you appear before me
Since eternity I have been a servant of wine and love
I have no grief over the stigma of unbelief
My head has found its gallows in you
I no longer search for the Holy Sanctuary
My head has found its gallows in you
I no longer search for the Holy Sanctuary
My worship is that worship which is not bound by the constraints of what is forbidden to others
My one glance at you, O God, is no less than formal prayer
Whatever brings you joy brings me joy
This is the miracle of my divine madness —
Wherever I bowed my head
There I made my Ka'ba
sections.explanation: This is the theological and emotional summit of the entire qawwali. The lover declares himself freed from the outward forms of religion — not from impiety but from a worship so total that it has transcended ritual. The image of the daar (gallows) is a direct invocation of Mansur al-Hallaj, the tenth-century Sufi martyr who declared 'Ana'l-Haqq' and was executed, yet went to the gallows in ecstasy, seeing in his death the ultimate union with God. The repeated couplet 'mere sar ko daar tera mil gaya / mujhe ab talaash-e-haram nahin' is among the most daring statements in Urdu Sufi poetry: I have found my gallows in you, and having found that, I need no Ka'ba. The closing miracle — 'jahan apne sar ko jhuka diya, wahan maine ka'ba bana diya' — is the completion of this logic: for the true lover, every act of prostration creates its own sacred geography. The Ka'ba is not a building in Mecca; it is wherever love bows its head.

sections.romanization:
Mere baad kisko sataoge
Kis kis ko sataoge mere baad
Umar bhar pachhtaoge tum mujh ko tukranay ke baad

sections.translation:
After me, whom will you torment?
Whom and whom will you torment after me?
You will repent your whole life after having cast me aside
Upon whom will you unleash your cruelty after I am gone?
You will remember my faithfulness
Weeping and weeping you will cry out in lament
You have already destroyed me — who else will you destroy?
sections.explanation: This verse marks one of the most dramatic tonal shifts in the qawwali — from ecstatic surrender to tender, heartbroken defiance. The lover is not angry but prophetic: he foresees the Beloved's regret with absolute clarity. On the Sufi level this verse operates simultaneously as the soul addressing its own nafs: after the self is annihilated in fana, what will the ego find to cling to? The repeated 'kis kis ko' (whom and whom) is a rhetorical device of escalating pathos, building communal emotion in the gathering and drawing the audience deeper into the lover's predicament through the power of identification.

sections.romanization:
Dil jalon se dil lagi achi nahin

sections.translation:
It is not wise to give your heart to those whose hearts already burn
It is not fitting to laugh with those who only know how to weep
In the very act of giving my heart, my heart was lost
The consequence of loving has now been received
I weep because my heart is gone —

Whom and whom will you torment after me?
sections.explanation: This verse introduces a note of philosophical rue — the lover reflecting on the inherent danger of ishq with a burning heart. The wordplay on 'dil lagi' (flirtation, attachment) and 'dil gaya' (the heart is gone) is characteristic of the Urdu poetic tradition's love of semantic compression: the very word for falling in love contains within it the announcement of loss. The sudden turn — 'tum kyun haste ho?' (why do you laugh?) — is a moment of raw confrontation, the lover catching the Beloved in a moment of amusement at his suffering. The verse closes by looping back to the 'mere baad' refrain, binding the two verses together into a single escalating emotional argument.

sections.translation:
When asked how rain falls —
They let drops of perspiration fall from their brow
When asked what magic lives inside music —
They spoke in tones so sweet the answer became the song
When asked how day and night find one another —
They let their tresses fall across their face
When asked how lightning strikes —
They met my gaze, and having met it, cast it down
When asked the condition of my own desires —
They extinguished a few burning candles
I kept saying: the punishment for the sin of love was well given
They built a world in my heart, then erased it
sections.explanation: This verse is a masterpiece of indirect expression — a series of questions about natural phenomena answered not in words but in gesture, each gesture a metaphor for a dimension of love's power. Rain is the sweat of longing on the brow; music's magic is the sweet speech of the Beloved; the meeting of day and night is the veil of hair falling between them; lightning is the devastating glance. The final image — candles extinguished when asked about desire — is the most devastating: the Beloved answers the question of the lover's hopes by dousing them one by one, and the lover's response is not bitterness but acceptance. 'Achi saza di' — a good punishment was given — is the ultimate statement of Sufi rida (contentment with divine decree): whatever the Beloved does, even destruction, is received as grace.

Tumhen ek qaatil bana diya
Mujhe dekho khwaahishen jaan-e-jaan
Main wohi hun Anwar-e-Meem Jaan
Tumhen itna khush tha jab kaha
Na chalaao is tarah tum zubaan
Bolo mera shukriya mehrban
Tumhen baat karna sikha diya
sections.translation:
Whom and whom will you torment after me, whom will you torment?
How will you erase me?
Where will you go to aim your arrows?
Take upon yourself the misfortunes of my friendship
Raise your hands and offer me your prayers
I have made of you a murderer
Look at me, O desires, O soul of my soul
I am that same Anwar-e-Meem Jaan
You were so pleased when told —
Do not wield your tongue this way
Say thank you to me, kind one
I have taught you how to speak
sections.explanation: This section represents one of the most remarkable features of Nusrat's live qawwali style — the seamless weaving of the 'mere baad' refrain back into the fabric of the performance after the 'jo poocha' verse, followed by a sudden pivot into playful, almost comedic self-reference. 'Balaen lena' is a ritual of deep love in South Asian tradition — taking upon oneself the evil eye or misfortune that threatens the beloved. The identification of the singer as 'Anwar-e-Meem Jaan' is a makhlas moment, the performer embedding a name within the performance as classical poets did in the final sher of a ghazal. The closing turn — scolding the Beloved for speaking harshly, demanding thanks for having taught them to speak — is Nusrat's signature humor, a deliberate comic deflation that releases the accumulated spiritual tension and paradoxically deepens the hal through laughter, a well-understood technique in the qawwali tradition.

sections.urdu_text:
یہ جو ہلکا ہلکا سرور ہے
یہ تِری نظر کا قصور ہے
کہ شراب پینا سکھا دیا
sections.romanization:
Yeh jo halka halka suroor hai
Yeh teri nazar ka qasoor hai
Keh sharaab peena sikha diya
sections.translation:
This gentle, gentle intoxication that lingers —
This is the fault of your gaze
That taught me how to drink
sections.explanation: The closing return to the refrain after the comedy of the Anwar-e-Meem Jaan passage is a masterstroke of qawwali architecture. The laughter has cleared the air; the gathering is now open and softened; and the refrain lands one final time with the accumulated weight of everything that has preceded it — the opening transgression, the cosmic intoxication, the theological audacity, the heartbreak, the humor. The 'halka halka' (gentle, gentle) of the title is the final word on the Sufi spiritual state: not the crash of wine, not the drama of mystical ecstasy, but a soft, persistent, indelible alteration — the soul that has once been touched by the divine gaze can never return to what it was before.
